text:
**Turned Around**

The maternity ward at St. Brendan's had been built, someone had told Nora, in the shape of a pinwheel, so that no nurse would ever be more than forty feet from any patient. This was meant to be comforting. At two in the morning, in a paper-thin gown and mesh underwear the size of a coffee filter, Nora found that it meant only that every corridor curved back toward the one she had just left. She passed the same framed print of a lighthouse three times.

Her son had been born at 4:12 the previous afternoon, after nineteen hours of labor that had ended in a flurry of competent voices and a sensation of being unzipped. Sometime after midnight a night nurse, a broad, soft-spoken woman whose badge said DOLORES, had wheeled the bassinet away. "You need four hours," Dolores said. "I'll bring him when he's hungry. You won't think you can sleep, and then you'll sleep." Nora had not slept. She had lain looking at the red numerals of the clock, and at some point she had gotten up and gone out to find her baby.

The hallway had the underwater hush of all hospitals at night. Machines sighed behind doors. A cart stood unattended with a single paper cup of ice chips on it, half melted. Nora drank the water, and it tasted of nothing, which seemed to her extraordinary.

At the end of the hall was a lounge with a vinyl couch, a television playing a cooking show with the sound off, and a woman sitting very upright with a sleeve of saltines in her lap.

"Is it Thursday?" the woman said.

"I think it's Thursday," Nora said. "It was Wednesday when I got here."

The woman was perhaps forty, with a long, pleasant, unfinished face and hair she had tied up with what looked like a hospital bracelet. "I keep thinking I left something on the stove," she said. "Isn't that funny? We don't even have a stove. We're between places."

"I keep thinking I forgot to feed the cat," Nora said, though they had no cat. They'd had a cat in college. She sat down on the other end of the couch, and the vinyl gave out a long, rude sound.

"Mine's in the nursery," the woman said after a while. "I went to look at her earlier, and I couldn't tell which one. Isn't that terrible? They were all wrapped up like burritos, all with the little hats, and I thought, well, that one's mine, and then I thought, but why that one." She laughed, a small dry laugh. "I'm sure it's the drugs."

"They said it would be like this," Nora said, though no one had said anything of the kind. What they had said, in the class she and Paul had attended in a church basement, was that she would feel *a rush of overwhelming love*. Nora had written it in the margin of her handout and underlined it, like an item on an exam.

She had felt a rush. That was the thing. When they laid him on her chest, slick and furious and the color of a plum, she had felt something enormous, and she had waited for it to resolve into a feeling she recognized. It hadn't. It had stayed enormous and unlabeled, like a piece of furniture delivered to the wrong address.

The woman offered her the sleeve of saltines, and Nora took one, and it was the best thing she had ever tasted.

---

She left the lounge and found, by some trick of the pinwheel, the nursery window. Two other women were already there, standing a little apart, with their hands pressed flat against the glass like people at an aquarium. One was very young, nineteen at most, with a shaved side of her head. The other was older and heavyset and wore a man's raincoat over her gown.

"Which one's yours?" the young one asked, without turning.

"I'm not sure I can see him from here," Nora said. This was true. The bassinets were lined up in two rows under a low, aqueous light, and she could see only a field of small striped bundles, each rising and falling with the same infinitesimal patience.

"They all look like him," the woman in the raincoat said. "That's what I can't get over. They all look like him, and they all look like nobody."

Behind the glass a nurse moved among the bassinets, lifting one, checking a wrist, setting it down.

"Everybody's a little turned around at this hour," said a voice at Nora's elbow, and she jumped. It was Dolores, or someone with Dolores's face, pushing the cart with the paper cup on it. "Back to bed, ladies. You'll thank me. He's on his way to you, hon," she added, to Nora, and then, in the same tone, to the girl with the shaved head, "And yours is on his way to you."

They all dispersed in different directions down the curving hall, trailing their IV poles or their private weather. Nora walked and walked and, quite suddenly, was standing in the doorway of her own room, 614, and the bassinet was already beside the bed, a small shape in a striped blanket, breathing.

She did not remember it being brought. She stood looking at it for some time. Then she got into bed and slept, at last, as Dolores had promised, as if she were falling down a well.

---

In the morning there was a great deal of light and a great deal of paper. A lactation consultant squeezed Nora's breast like a stone fruit. Nobody said anything about the night. It was as though the night had been a rumor.

Paul arrived at ten with a bag of clothes and the glassy cheerfulness he put on in emergencies. He had spent the night, he told her, on the floor of the apartment with the car seat, trying to install it according to a video. Then he went to the bassinet and looked down for a long time, with his hands hanging at his sides. "Hi, buddy," he said. "Hi. It's me."

A nurse who was not Dolores came to cut off the bracelets. Nora's came off easily. The baby's was a ring of white plastic on an ankle no thicker than a thumb, and the nurse snipped it and dropped it into the pocket of her scrubs with a casualness that Nora would turn over for weeks afterward. She did not look at it. She was, at that moment, looking at the baby's face.

It was not that she knew, right away. It was that something in her, some low and sensible animal, lifted its head. The baby in her arms, being buckled by Paul into a snowsuit the color of a traffic cone, had a pointed little chin. Her son, the plum-colored one, had had a round face and a crease in the rim of his left ear, as though it had been folded for safekeeping. She was sure of the ear. She had stroked it with her thumb for the first hour of his life and thought, *I will know that ear anywhere.* This ear was flat and perfect. This baby had a fuzz of dark hair that came to a point on the forehead, and when he opened his eyes they were an unfocused, drowned-looking gray, and he looked not at her but past her, at something near the ceiling, with an expression of mild and absolute attention.

"He's so alert," Paul said.

"Yes," Nora said.

She could have said it then. She could have said it a dozen times: in the room, with the nurse right there; in the elevator; at the front desk, where a volunteer in a pink smock handed her a bag of samples. She stood in the lobby with the baby against her shoulder and the whole apparatus of correction arranged itself in her mind, tidy and complete: *There's been a mistake. This isn't ours.* It was a sentence of six words. She could feel its weight in her mouth, like a pit in an olive.

And then, across the lobby, she saw the woman from the lounge.

The woman stood by the revolving door with a man in a Mets cap and an enormous bouquet, and in the crook of her arm she held a baby in a striped blanket. Her hair was down, and it was lovely, and she looked, in the stunned winter light through the glass, like a person who has been told wonderful news in a language she does not speak. She saw Nora. For a moment they only looked at each other across thirty feet of speckled linoleum. The woman's eyes went to the bundle on Nora's shoulder, and then back to Nora's face, and something passed over her own that Nora understood completely and would never be able to describe, a kind of vast, helpless courtesy.

Then the woman smiled. It was not a smile of apology or of complicity. It was the smile of someone at a wedding who has just realized that she is happy.

She lifted two fingers from the blanket, a small salute. Then the revolving door took her, and the man in the cap, and the bouquet, and the baby, and put them out on the sidewalk in the cold.

"Ready?" said Paul.

"Ready," Nora said.

---

It was a bright, hard, ordinary day. Paul drove at eleven miles an hour with the hazards on, and Nora sat in the back beside the baby, who slept with his fist against his cheek, and watched the city go by in its usual indifference: a bus advertising a personal-injury lawyer, a dog in a sweater.

She thought, *I should call.* She thought it with great clarity, in the same voice in which she thought *I should call the dentist.* There would be a number, a risk manager, a form, a hushed hallway of consequence. Somewhere across the city another woman was presumably unbuckling another seat, and looking down, and having the same thought, or not having it.

What astonished her was that she wasn't afraid. She waited for the fear the way she had waited, in the delivery room, for the love, and what arrived instead was a lightness, a spreading warmth under the breastbone, as though she'd been handed, unasked, a key to a house she had always suspected she owned. She looked at the pointed chin, the dark crest of hair. The small, serious, gray eyes had opened again and were regarding her, directly, with the courteous attention of a stranger on a train.

"Hello," she said. "Who are you?"

He yawned, a huge, silent, pink event.

"He looks like you," Paul said, to the rearview mirror. "Doesn't he? Around the mouth."

"Around the mouth," she agreed.

At home the radiator was knocking, and the apartment had the stale, expectant air of a place prepared for a visitor. Nora laid the baby in the middle of their bed, on the white comforter, and unwrapped him one layer at a time, until he lay in just his diaper with his arms thrown up beside his head like a man surrendering. She looked at his heels, at the creases of his knees, at the whorl of hair on the crown of his head, which went clockwise. She did not know which way her son's had gone. She realized that she had never looked.

That was the part she would have trouble explaining, later, in the long blue hours when she walked the apartment with him against her shoulder, and the lights of other people's kitchens came on across the airshaft one by one. It was not that she had decided to keep him. It was that the question seemed to have been asked in a language she had stopped speaking at some point during the night, somewhere between the saltines and the glass. What she knew was that her arms had known the weight of him at once, and gone on knowing it. What she knew was that the happiness was real, and unearned, and had nothing to do with whose he was, and was therefore possibly the purest happiness she had ever been given.

She would call tomorrow, she told herself. Or the day after, when she had slept.

On the bed the baby turned his head toward her voice, though she had not said anything, and opened his mouth, and Nora, who had been carrying herself carefully for nine months and nineteen hours and one long night, sat down on the edge of the comforter and let herself be found.
